root.note: The usual explanation, followed by Wiktionary for trabalhar: Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre ‘to torture’, from tripālium. The tripālium itself is barely attested and the link has been questioned, so the story is told with caution.

stages.meaning: to suffer, to toil; pain, effort

history: The most famous explanation of trabalho is a dark one. A tripālium, ‘three stakes’, was a device used to hold or torture someone, and a verb *tripāliāre, ‘to torment’, is thought to lie behind Old Portuguese traballar, ‘to suffer, to toil’. Early uses of the noun do mean pain and hardship, and only later plain work. The story is widely repeated, but the evidence for the tripālium is thin and some scholars doubt the link, so it is best enjoyed with care. What is clear is that Latin labor and opus lost out. Today trabalho is your job, your work and your workplace: vou para o trabalho, ‘I'm going to work’. Spanish trabajo and French travail are the same word.
historyEinfach: Trabalho means ‘work’ or ‘job’. The word is old and first meant ‘pain, hard effort’. Many books say it comes from a Latin word for a device with three stakes, used to hurt people. Experts are not sure about this. Spanish trabajo and French travail are the same word.

elsewhere.text: Medieval journeys were hard work, and English travel comes from the French word for toil.
French has the same word for work, and also kept the old sense: a woman in labour is en travail.
